headline: Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass
border_caption: The morning after Kristallnacht: Germans walk past the shattered windows of a Jewish-owned shop, November 10, 1938.

image.note: Passersby look away from destroyed Jewish shops on November 10, 1938, the day after Kristallnacht.

hook: November 9, 1938: Kristallnacht, the “Night of Broken Glass.” Ten months before World War II began, Nazi Germany showed the world exactly where it was heading.
body: The pretext was the death of German diplomat Ernst vom Rath, shot in Paris by Herschel Grynszpan, a 17-year-old Polish Jew whose family had just been expelled from Germany. That night, Nazi stormtroopers and Hitler Youth attacked Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland.

They smashed the windows of about 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses and destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms. At least 91 Jews were murdered. Some 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to the concentration camps at Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen.

Many Germans simply looked away, as the people in this photograph seem to. Kristallnacht marked the moment Nazi persecution of the Jews turned into open, organized violence, on the road that led to the Holocaust.
